Don't read the following if you don't care about my situation, just give me some advice on being a good boss, please.

I just had an employee put in her 3 week notice this morning. She is in a salaried position, and we just hit a huge busy streak and we're short-staffed until this Wednesday.

She left early last week without telling me to run errands with her boyfriend, knowing we had a longer day. I gave her about a week's warning that we will be busy for a few weeks and that she will have to stay late some day (6 or 7 p.m.), but that I would work with her to get her out of early on other days. I also told her early last week that she would have to work this coming weekend (we usually work one or two weekends a month), there is too much work that HAS to be done for our clients on those days.

She got upset about working this weekend because she wanted to go to the lake. I told her she is on salary, this isn't a normal thing and I need her help. I even offered a bonus at the end of the quarter for all of the extra work she will have to put in this month. I also looked at the schedule and texted her yesterday to let her know she can take off this Wednesday and Thursday in exchange for working this weekend.

Last week was her busiest week since starting with me, and she had to work a whopping 42 hours. Yes, she is on salary but generally only works maybe 35 hours a week. I have been telling her for months this time of year is busy for us, and have given her several 3-day weekends. Since she's now a manager, I've tried to give her projects when it's slow, like come up with some new marketing ideas and write out her plans for training a new hire. We even talked Friday about getting her an office in a different county that she wants to move to in a few years.

Then, today she tells me she's quitting. Supposedly got a job at the post office, but I never got a call to verify employment. Also, she's only been a manager since the beginning of this month, why would she take the promotion if she was waiting to hear about another job? Like we went 2 weeks ago and got her a business debit card and she got business cards to hand out to people at the beginning of July.

I try to be a good boss, and treat employees how I'd like to be treated. There are times when I can be a bitch, but they are few and far between, and when I realize my behavior I apologize and stop it. I am trying to hard to be a good boss, but I wonder if I'm too "friendly" and people take advantage of it; then when there's a rush they don't want to work. I have a feeling the whole "having to work this weekend" ordeal is what is making her quit.

There have been some problems, such as insubordination on her part as well as her slacking on the job in the past. I asked a former co-worker of hers if she ever treated their last boss the same way, and he was shocked she would talk to me like that.

Bear with me...I'm texting this response.

First, I wonder how clear you are in setting expectations on anyone that you hire into this role or promote. Specifically, do you outline the scheduling needs and expectations of the seasonal demands as they change and the expectation to step-up to the plate and work weekends? There is no way I'd pay a salaried person extra for working extra during our busy season. If we're on a commission structure that's different. If we meet/exceed annual goals that's different.

Instead of adding another layer of supervisor and worrying about why this person doesn't like you, have you evaluated your current organizational structure? How many people report to you now? Are there duties that can be spread out among your current team?

Mixplate makes some great points in terms of managing through change and exit interviewing. Re-read those. While weekly check-ins can be demanding until you make them a habit they are worthwhile. My favorite questions to ask 1) how are things going this week? 2) what more can I be doing for you? And finally 3) what's on your plate and how are you moving along towards target deadlines? I try not to be a pain in the ass but my direct reports need to earn their independence based on their productivity and follow-through. When they're on top is their game I steer clear, when they're struggling I make myself available.

On a different note, in this particular case - do you absolutely need this person? Because three weeks notice is great but what kind of commitment and productivity will you actually get during this time? You may want to make a transition plan where this person uses the time they have these three weeks to train others on the team. And if you can delay your promotion/hiring decision you can reallocate funds to reward others on your team for rallying together and making shit happen.
